item.title: Zahid: Harmonious environment essential for development
item.description:
Women and Children Affairs and Social Welfare Minister Dr AZM Zahid Hossain on Saturday stressed the need for maintaining unity and harmony among the people for development, saying that development in any area is possible only through unity, not conflicts.
“A sound and peaceful environment serves as a key prerequisite for development. If there are divisions, clashes and conflicts among the people, development activities are obstructed. But a cordial and harmonious environment facilitates development,” he said while speaking at a workers’ conference and views-exchange meeting organized by Joypur Union unit of Nawabganj upazila BNP in Dinajpur.
Addressing the local leaders and activists of the BNP, Zahid said, “If you maintain a good environment in your area, it will be easier to carry out development activities at all levels. But if conflicts arise among you, development activities will be obstructed.”
The minister stressed the need to educate children properly and develop them as competent citizens. “We have to work together to build the future generation on the foundation of humanity and moral values. Alongside ensuring a favorable environment for education, social awareness must be increased to guide the younger generation in the right direction,” he said.
“If we fail to do something good for the future generation, we will not be able to protect them from the devastating situation caused by drugs,” he added. Calling for a united social resistance against drug abuse, the minister said people involved in drug trafficking must be resisted collectively and their unethical activities stopped.
“Simply sitting at home and waiting for law enforcement agencies will not be enough to eliminate the presence of drugs in society,” he said. The minister also said it is the responsibility of society to stand beside any individual or family facing an economic crisis.

item.title: Dengue cases surge in Chittagong despite control measures
item.description:
Dengue cases have continued to rise in Chittagong, with 760 infections recorded in the first 12 days of September.
According to the Civil Surgeon’s Office, 2,795 dengue cases have been reported in Chittagong from January to September 12. Of them, 1,214 patients are from Chittagong city, 1,234 from different upazilas and 349 from other districts under the division.
Ten people have died of the mosquito-borne disease, while 262 patients are currently receiving treatment in different hospitals. Chittagong Medical College Hospital has the highest number of dengue patients.
Monthly figures show a sharp increase during the monsoon. The district recorded 68 cases in January, 22 in February, 20 in March, 29 in April, 37 in May, 122 in June, 534 in July, 1,206 in August and 760 in the first 11 days of September.
Among the 15 upazilas, Sitakunda recorded the highest number of cases at 355, followed by Karnaphuli with 195, Banshkhali 95, Rangunia 83, Raozan 67, Patiya 62, Boalkhali 49, Hathazari 37 and Mirsarai 36.
The Chittagong City Corporation (CCC) has launched a special mosquito-control campaign as dengue cases rise. A survey by its health department identified 155 potential Aedes breeding grounds across the city, including educational institutions, construction sites, abandoned buildings and residential areas.
CCC officials said eight wards have been identified as dengue hotspots. Insecticides are being sprayed at the homes of dengue patients and within a 500-metre radius.
Malaria and Mosquito Control Officer Md Sarful Islam Mahi said breeding sites have been destroyed and insecticides applied in the identified hotspots.
Civil Surgeon Dr Mohammad Sajedur Rahman said dengue prevention requires both mosquito control and the destruction of Aedes breeding grounds. He said the health department has asked the city corporation to intensify mosquito-control activities.
CCC Executive Officer and Secretary Ashraful Amin said the corporation is using BTI to destroy mosquito larvae, alongside fogging to kill adult mosquitoes. More than 100 workers have received special training for the campaign.

item.title: Rajshahi takes dengue fight to the grassroots
item.description:
Rajshahi Divisional Commissioner Yusuf Ali on Saturday called for turning dengue prevention and cleanliness activities into a social movement by encouraging people to keep their own surroundings clean.
“We must not remain dependent only on cleaners for maintaining cleanliness; rather, we need to develop the habit of cleaning our own spaces ourselves,” he said.
He made the remarks while attending a live telecast of the nationwide dengue prevention and cleanliness campaign inaugurated by Prime Minister Tarique Rahman at the South Plaza of the National Parliament Building.
The programme was screened through a video conference at the conference room of the Rajshahi Deputy Commissioner’s Office.
The divisional commissioner said extensive initiatives have been taken in Rajshahi as part of the three-month nationwide dengue prevention and cleanliness campaign announced by the prime minister.
In the first phase, cleanliness drives are being conducted at government offices. Educational institutions, religious institutions, dengue hotspots and drains in municipalities and city corporations across the division will gradually be brought under the campaign, he said.
Yusuf Ali said necessary instructions have been issued to Upazila Nirbahi Officers (UNOs) to implement the campaign at the grassroots level.
Initiatives have also been taken to remove stagnant water from rooftops, flower tubs and other potential mosquito-breeding sites around homes and offices, while ensuring proper cleanliness of the premises.
Volunteer organisations, including Girls Guide, Scouts and BD Clean, have been engaged to turn the campaign into a mass initiative.
The virtual conference was attended by Deputy Commissioner Kazi Shahidul Islam and Superintendent of Police Mamun Or Rashid, along with government and non-government officials and employees, teachers and students, scouts and journalists.
Following the programme, the divisional commissioner formally inaugurated the dengue prevention and cleanliness campaign in Rajshahi by participating in a cleaning drive at the premises of the Divisional Commissioner’s and Deputy Commissioner’s offices.
Earlier, a colourful rally was brought out from the Deputy Commissioner’s Office premises. The rally paraded through important roads in the city before returning to the same venue.

item.title: Four-decade-old bridge poses accident risk in Taraganj
item.description:
A bridge over the Sarmangla River in Rangpur’s Taraganj upazila has become unfit for traffic after nearly four decades without proper repairs, raising fears of major accidents.
The bridge is the only route connecting Shailbari and nine neighboring villages under Alampur Union. Around 25,000 people, including students, farmers, laborers and other professionals, use the bridge regularly.
A recent visit found most of the bridge’s railings broken or completely missing. The structure, only about 3.5 feet wide, has virtually no safety barriers on either side. Plaster has peeled off the pillars, exposing reinforcement rods, while several potholes have developed on its surface.
The dilapidated bridge can no longer safely accommodate vehicles other than motorcycles and bicycles. Rickshaws, vans and auto-rickshaws have to cross the bridge at considerable risk, while ambulances and microbuses cannot use it because of its narrow width.
Farmers from the surrounding villages are among the worst affected. They struggle to transport rice, vegetables and other agricultural produce to local markets and are often forced to take longer alternative routes, increasing transportation costs.
Madrasa teacher Eshramul Haque of Shailbari said the bridge was too narrow for regular vehicular movement. “Rickshaws, vans, microbuses and auto-rickshaws cannot cross it,” he said.
Lokman Hossain of Dangapara said the bridge shakes when people cross it. “The railings are broken and the pillars have developed cracks. Only Allah knows when it may collapse,” he said.
Local schoolteacher Momtaz Uddin said farmers and young students were suffering the most because of the bridge’s condition.
Aminur Rahman, an elderly resident, said locals had repeatedly sought repairs from MPs, union council chairmen and members over the past 15-16 years, but received only assurances.
Taraganj LGED engineer Nafiur Rahman said a proposal had been sent to the district authorities for reconstruction of the bridge. He said construction of a permanent bridge would begin once the required budget and project approval were secured, but he could not say when work would start.

item.title: Plastic waste threatens Sundarbans as tides carry coastal pollution into forest
item.description:
Plastic waste discarded by coastal communities and sea-going fishermen is increasingly being carried by tides into the Sundarbans, posing a growing threat to its fragile ecosystem and biodiversity.
Single-use plastic bottles, food packets, polythene bags, fishing-related materials and pesticide containers are accumulating along the forest’s rivers, canals and tourist destinations. Environmentalists and tourism operators say the crisis cannot be addressed by raising awareness among tourists alone. Coastal communities, fishermen, local businesses and government agencies must also be involved.
The Tour Operators Association of Sundarbans (TOAS) removed around 15 sacks of plastic waste from five tourist spots during a three-day cleanup campaign from September 7 to 9. The waste was collected from the forest and transported to Khulna for disposal.
TOAS had carried out a similar campaign at the same locations in May, when the tourism season was closed, removing 12 sacks of plastic waste. Despite the absence of tourists for nearly four months, large quantities of plastic had accumulated again. The latest cleanup also uncovered numerous glass bottles believed to have been used for pesticides.
Forest officials say much of the waste is not necessarily generated inside the forest. Instead, it is carried from coastal areas through rivers and tidal currents.
Tourists generally come to the Sundarbans with some awareness about environmental protection. Now it is equally important to create awareness among coastal communities and sea-going fishermen, forest officials said.
Plastic discarded into canals, rivers and coastal waterways is eventually carried into the Sundarbans by the ebb and flow of tides. Katka, Kachikhali, Jamtala, Dimer Char and Andharmanik are among the forest’s most popular tourist destinations, where plastic bottles, packets, polythene bags and fishing-related waste are increasingly visible.
The tourism season began on September 1, and TOAS launched its cleanup campaign at the beginning of the season. The association normally conducts cleanup drives twice a year, but the volume of waste found this year has prompted members to consider continuing the initiative throughout the season. They plan to collect plastic during regular trips and bring it back on their vessels for proper disposal.
The problem extends far beyond the forest. Plastic and polythene use is rising across coastal districts including Khulna, Bagerhat, Satkhira, Patuakhali and Barguna. Single-use plates, cups, spoons, bottles and food packaging have become common at roadside eateries, tea stalls, restaurants and social gatherings. Much of this waste is discarded beside canals, ponds and rivers, allowing tidal currents to carry it towards the Sundarbans.
Research has also highlighted the extent of microplastic contamination in the coastal ecosystem. A study titled Spatial Distribution and Characterization of Microplastics in the Coastal Water and Sediment of the Bay of Bengal Coast, Bangladesh, conducted between 2020 and 2022 by a Khulna University student, found microplastics in coastal water, sediment, snails and fish. The study recorded an average of 2.22 microplastic items per litre of water in the Sundarbans and 734 items per kilogram of sediment. Microplastics were also detected in snails and marine fish.
At Dimer Char, plastic waste was found scattered from the beach deep into the forest, while fishing-related plastic was seen floating in with sea currents. Large quantities were removed from Katka and Kachikhali during the latest cleanup. Although the two-kilometre walking trail at Jamtala was relatively clean, significant amounts of plastic were found along the adjacent beach.
Plastic waste is also widespread around markets and settlements in Satkhira’s coastal areas, including Atulia, Gabura, Burigoalini, Munshiganj and Kaikhali. Discarded tea cups, food containers and snack packets are commonly seen along riverbanks in Munshiganj, Nawabeki and Nildumur, as well as around Mongla.
Fishermen say plastic pollution is affecting both their livelihoods and the natural environment. Bacchu Hossain of Datinakhali village in Shyamnagar said plastic had become a regular part of his catch.
“Now, when we cast our nets in the river, we often get chips packets, water bottles and polythene instead of fish,” he said, adding that fish stocks had declined compared with the past.
Another fisherman, Ashik Hossain of Gabura, said plastic was also covering chars where weeds and small plants once grew. He said fishermen often had nowhere to store bottles and food packets because there were no waste bins at landing points or on boats.
Tourists have raised similar concerns. Rahman Mia, who visited Kachikhali with his family from Rajshahi, said tourists should avoid littering but need proper facilities to dispose of waste. Student Samia Haque of Pabna said seeing plastic in the forest was upsetting and stressed that local communities also needed greater awareness.
TOAS members say tourism operators should not be blamed entirely for the pollution. They argue that inadequate waste-management systems in coastal communities are a major source of the problem. TOAS General Secretary Mazharul Haque Kochi said the association had stopped using single-use plastics on its vessels and was counselling tourists about responsible waste disposal.
Sundarbans East Forest Division Divisional Forest Officer Md Rezaul Karim said carrying or disposing of plastic inside the forest is strictly prohibited. However, he said the Forest Department and TOAS cannot solve the problem alone.
He called for coordinated action involving local administrations, the Department of Environment and coastal communities. Sundarbans West Forest Division DFO AZM Hasanur Rahman also welcomed the cleanup initiative and said forest personnel would remove plastic during regular patrols.
With plastic continuing to arrive through the tides, stakeholders say the Sundarbans needs a comprehensive waste-management system extending beyond the forest—from coastal markets and settlements to fishing boats and tourist vessels.
Without coordinated action, the steady flow of plastic could become a long-term threat to one of Bangladesh’s most important natural ecosystems and its vital natural shield against coastal disasters.

item.title: Hi-tech parks: PPRC discussion examines gap between mission and reality
item.description:
The Power and Participation Research Centre (PPRC) on Saturday held an episode of its Ajker Agenda virtual series titled “Hi-Tech Parks: What is the Mission? What is the Reality?”, bringing together industry leaders, former officials and policy experts to assess the performance of Bangladesh’s High-Tech and Software Technology Parks.
The discussion focused on why, despite the establishment of dozens of parks and rising budget allocations, the sector has yet to deliver results comparable to similar initiatives in other countries, and what is needed to bridge the gap between the parks’ original mission and their performance on the ground.
Dr M Rokonuzzaman, professor of the Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering at North South University, said Bangladesh established 39 High-Tech and Software Technology Parks between 2009 and 2023 on the assumption that infrastructure alone would drive investment and create a hi-tech boom.
“Bangladesh built 39 High-Tech and Software Technology Parks between 2009 and 2023 on the assumption that infrastructure alone would trigger a hi-tech boom and investment without effective focus on a supportive ecosystem, availability of skilled labour, and industry-academia linkage. Results so far clearly show that the assumption was not the right one, as the examples of Taiwan, South Korea, Malaysia and Singapore attest,” he said.
Mohammad Mohidul Islam, managing director of Ongsho, gave a critical assessment of the Jessore High-Tech Park, established in December 2017.
“The 40 companies currently housed in the park struggle independently for survival without effective ecosystem support. The authority treats them as tenants rather than as entrepreneurs. Trained manpower quickly leaves. Maintenance of the facility is very poor, and the costs of utilities are high,” he said.
Engr Md Ashafuddoza Shishir, co-founder and chief operating officer of Netro Systems Ltd and Telzen at Hi-Tech Park Rajshahi, offered a more positive assessment of the Rajshahi experience. He pointed to the growth of technology ventures that emerged from a 2016 incubation centre and have since developed international operations.
He, however, said: “The tangible benefit for companies in the Rajshahi Hi-Tech Park remains confined to tax exemptions, as direct authority support for startups is largely absent.”
Farhana A Rahman, chairperson and CEO of UY Systems Ltd, drawing on her experience with BASIS, said the country remained caught in a cycle of ambitious promises without sufficient progress on the ground.
“We remain trapped in a loop of grandiose promises about high-tech parks, yet despite the building of so many parks across the country, real progress on the ground remains absent. The Kaliakor Hi-Tech Park offered land plots but no supportive services, so that many later surrendered their plot allocations,” she said.
Rafel Kabir, managing director of DNS Software Ltd, attributed many of the sector’s shortcomings to government policy and sensationalist media coverage. He contrasted the light-touch regulatory environment that allowed services such as Uber and Foodpanda to expand with the top-down approach taken in developing the parks.
“Rather than relying solely on export tax incentives, High-Tech Parks should have targeted foundational technology manufacturing, like motherboard and chip fabrication, while delivering complete, EPZ-grade infrastructure,” he said.
Faiz Ahmad Taiyeb, former special assistant to the Chief Adviser of Bangladesh at the Ministry of Posts, Telecommunications and Information Technology, reflected on his experience overseeing the sector and identified the location of the parks as a major factor behind their limited impact.
“The core failure of Bangladesh’s High-Tech Parks stems from placing heavy physical infrastructure in regions lacking a viable local economy,” he said, adding that the challenges extend beyond physical infrastructure to the credibility and effectiveness of the training ecosystem.
Summing up the discussion, moderator Hossain Zillur Rahman, executive chairman of PPRC, said: “Long-term success requires shifting focus from building physical real estate to cultivating soft infrastructure, skilled human capital, and industry-driven training.”
The discussion concluded that Bangladesh does not necessarily need to abandon the High-Tech Park model but must strengthen the foundations on which the parks operate, including reliable utilities, accountable governance and effective support systems that treat companies as partners rather than tenants.

PM to distribute 7,000 farmer cards in Feni on Thursday
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman will distribute 7000 farmers' cards in Feni on September 17, as the government has set a target to distribute 16.5 million cards among farmers over the next four years, with an estimated initial cost of Taka 681 crore.
Fisheries, Livestock and Agriculture minister Mohammad Amin Ur Rashid said this after visiting Fulgazi government Pilot High School playground, where the prime minister will distribute the cards, on Saturday morning.
Under the target, the government will distribute the farmer cards among 1.10 lakh farmers across the country on that day.
Simultaneous launching ceremonies will be held in 50 districts on the same day. Bank accounts have already been opened for one lakh of the 16.30 lakh farmers registered under the program so far, ministry officials said.
Under the cash incentive program, landless, marginal and small farmers holding the card will receive Tk2,500 directly through their bank accounts. Around one lakh farmers are expected to receive the incentive on the inauguration day.
Information on another five lakh farmers has already been verified and approved for opening bank accounts, the ministry said.
“The farmer cards will be distributed in each upazila and union, and the card will be distributed among all the farmers within the scheduled time”, the minister told the function.
The government has decided to bring farmers under the card system to make subsidies, loans, and incentives more accessible to them in the agriculture sector.
Regarding the fertilizer stock, the agriculture minister said the country has no crisis of fertilizer, as a ‘vicious circle’ is trying to create anarchy in the fertilizer distribution system.
The program will be implemented in three stages – pre-pilot, pilot and nationwide expansion. In the pre-pilot phase, farmers engaged in crop production, fisheries and livestock, including dairy farmers, will be included across 11 blocks in 11 upazilas of 10 districts.
According to the ministry, the pre-pilot phase of the Farmer's Card distribution program has already been launched on Pohela Boishakh, the first day of the Bangla New Year on April 14 this year.
In the first phase, 22,065 farmers in 11 upazilas under 10 districts received the cards. Of them, 20,671 landless, marginal, and small farmers received Tk2,500 annually in direct cash assistance.
The Agriculture Ministry aims to distribute Farmer Cards to 43 lakh farmers during the 2026-27 fiscal year, out of an estimated 2.27 crore farmers nationwide.
The remaining farmers will gradually be brought under the program, according to the ministry.
Additional Secretary of the agriculture ministry Md Yasin, Director General of the Department of Agricultural Extension (DAE) Md Abdur Rahim, Deputy Commissioner of Feni Mohammad Mahbubul Karim, Fulgazi Upazila Nirbahi Officer Md Kawser Hamid, Fulgazi Upazila assistant commissioner (land) Soheli Nawshin Protasha, BNP national executive committee assistant secretary Belal Hossen, BNP national executive committee member Abu Taleb, and Upazila BNP convener Fakhrul Alam Swapan were also present during this time.

item.title: Dismembered body parts of woman found in Adabor
item.description:
Police recovered the severed head and hand of an unidentified woman from Adabor in the capital on Saturday.
The body parts were recovered in a sack from the Hakkar Mor area of Adabor-10, said Adabor Police Station Officer-in-Charge (OC) Zahidul Islam.
He said police went to the spot after receiving information from locals and recovered the body parts. The woman’s legs have yet to be found.
Her identity could not be immediately ascertained. Police are also yet to determine the motive for the killing or identify those responsible.
Efforts are underway to identify those involved and uncover the circumstances behind the murder, the OC said.

item.title: China, Russia, Iran leaders gather in India as BRICS nations seek common ground
item.description:
Chinese President Xi Jinping joined the leaders of Russia, Iran, India and other BRICS nations in New Delhi on Saturday, seeking common ground on the Middle East war as deep divisions test the 11-member bloc.
Xi told the summit that the Middle East war “does not serve the common interests of the international community,” according to Chinese state news agency Xinhua.
Foreign ministers of the BRICS grouping failed to agree on a joint statement when they met in New Delhi in May, with Iran, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates divided over the war that began with US-Israeli strikes on February 28.
However, Indian diplomatic sources said leaders were working towards a joint position on some issues as the bloc seeks to bolster its global influence and address conflict, trade turbulence and energy security.
BRICS was created in 2009 as a forum for major emerging economies seeking greater influence in institutions dominated by Western powers.
“We have to transform this pyramid of privilege into a platform of partnership,” Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi told Xi, Russian President Vladimir Putin, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and other leaders.
Modi, opening the two-day summit, called for a system “where every country has a voice, every member has a stake, and humanity’s development is at the centre of every effort.”
He told leaders that BRICS nations “represent 50% of the world’s population, 40% of global GDP, and more than 25% of global trade.”
The Middle East conflict was high on the agenda.
India maintains cordial relations with Iran and Israel, but is also careful to strike a delicate balance in its ties with Washington.
Iran’s Pezeshkian attended the summit shortly after warning that the Middle East does not need the United States to be a “regional policeman,” with the two countries at war and tensions threatening the vital Strait of Hormuz.
UAE President Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan is also at the summit in New Delhi, as is Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi, and Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan is expected to join later on Saturday.
India has navigated the energy crisis caused by the US-Iran war in part by turning to Russia, despite Moscow’s war in Ukraine and pressure from Washington and other Western capitals.
Modi embraced Putin before talks on Friday. Putin, who last visited India in December 2025, is one of New Delhi’s most important strategic partners.
But the summit’s other major focus is China.
Xi’s visit is also being closely watched because it is his first to neighboring India since 2019, and the biggest step yet in a cautious thaw between the nuclear-armed rivals.
Xi was given a red-carpet welcome, with an honor guard of soldiers and traditional dancers in colorful dresses, and greeted with a handshake by Modi at the summit venue.
His visit comes six years after a deadly military clash along their disputed Tibetan border, with ties gradually improving through restored flights, visas and high-level contacts.
Beijing said ahead of his visit that it was “ready to work with India... by strengthening communication, enhancing cooperation, and properly handling differences.”
The underlying territorial dispute remains unresolved, and both sides retain heavy military deployments along their roughly 3,500-kilometre (2,175-mile) high-altitude border with Tibet.
Xi is due to hold face-to-face talks with Modi later on Saturday, according to New Delhi’s foreign ministry.
“They are looking for ‘early and substantial harvest’ when it comes to the border issue,” said Pradeep Taneja, a China-India expert at the University of Melbourne.
“You cannot have a build-up of your forces on the border... but at the same time say ‘we should continue to have people-to-people relations and economic relationships.’”
Deep mistrust remains, with their contested Himalayan frontier, a widening trade deficit and strategic rivalry continuing to complicate ties.
Dozens of Tibetans protested in New Delhi on Friday -- exiles, like their Buddhist leader the Dalai Lama, who has lived in India since fleeing a Chinese crackdown in 1959 -- waving placards against Xi’s visit.

item.title: Zelensky says willing to meet Putin at G20 in Miami
item.description:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said he would be willing to meet Russian President Vladimir Putin at a G20 summit in December, in an interview released Saturday, as efforts intensify to end the conflict.
Washington is seeking to kick-start long-stalled negotiations to find a solution to the conflict, Europe’s deadliest since World War II, with US negotiators recently visiting Kyiv and Moscow and President Donald Trump and Putin this week holding talks on the conflict over the phone.
The United States holds this year’s presidency of the Group of 20 major economies, which comprises 19 countries plus the European Union and the African Union, and culminates in a leaders’ summit in Miami in December.
Russia’s finance minister has already attended one G20 meeting, causing discomfort among some of Ukraine’s allies, and a Russian diplomat said Saturday that Moscow will also send some officials to a G20 energy meeting in Houston next week.
Asked whether he would be willing to meet Putin at the December summit if both leaders were invited, Zelensky told German broadcaster Deutsche Welle: “Yes, of course.”
“We have to come. We have to meet, to speak, and make decisions.
“It’s not about words. What I will tell him or what he wants to tell me, it doesn’t matter. It doesn’t matter. Matters only result. Result matters. That’s it.”
Last weekend, US negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner visited Moscow and Putin and Trump also discussed the war earlier in the week in what the Kremlin termed an “extremely frank” and constructive hour-long phone call.
In the Deutsche Welle interview, which took place Friday in Canada, Zelensky said that Witkoff and Kushner’s visit was a “good signal,” and it was important the pair had visited Kyiv as well as Moscow.
“It’s respect to our people,” he said.
Zelensky has also announced he plans to meet Trump in late September, as Washington pushes for fresh face-to-face talks between Moscow and Kyiv.
Asked about Ukraine’s position ahead of possible negotiations, Zelensky responded: “Ukraine now is much stronger than last year on the battlefield.”
Russia was sustaining heavy battlefield losses, paying a “big price” for “very slow moves on the battlefield.” he said.
“That’s why we think that we have a good position for negotiations.”
Kyiv has said the talks could happen as early as this month, but the Kremlin on Monday said it was “too early” to discuss a venue or dates.
Several previous rounds of negotiations have failed. Trust between the sides is low, and there is no sign that Moscow or Kyiv have shifted their positions.
Both Moscow and Kyiv have escalated long-range strikes on each other in recent months, leading to the highest civilian death toll since the early days of the war.
Zelensky also repeated his call for Ukraine’s allies to provide more interceptor missiles to fend off Russian air attacks.
“Russia produces... today 140 ballistic missiles per month. So, according to the rules of Nato, if you want to destroy 140, you need 280... You will never have 280 missiles per month,” he said.
It was a “huge challenge” to have 100 a month, he said.

item.title: Chhatra Dal announces nationwide two-day cleanliness drive
item.description:
Bangladesh Jatiyatabadi Chhatra Dal will conduct a two-day cleanliness drive across the country to raise awareness about dengue prevention.
The organisation’s President Rakibul Islam Rakib and General Secretary Nasir Uddin Nasir have called on its leaders, activists and students to participate in the program at educational institutions nationwide on Sunday and Monday.
The information was disclosed in a press release issued on Saturday and signed by Office Secretary, also a vice-president, Md Jahangir Alam.
According to the release, a three-month “Dengue Prevention and Cleanliness Campaign-2026” began nationwide on Saturday to raise public awareness about dengue prevention and promote a clean environment.
As part of the campaign, Chhatra Dal has announced the special two-day program at educational institutions across the country to eliminate mosquito breeding grounds, ensure cleanliness and create a safe and healthy academic environment for students.

item.title: Chhatra Dal leader missing after falling into Padma River
item.description:
A local leader of Jatiyatabadi Chhatra Dal (JCD) went missing after falling into the Padma River when a boat carrying 123 people hit a pillar of the Hardinge Bridge in Bheramara upazila of Kushtia district on Friday night.
The Chhatra Dal leader was identified as Rakibuzzaman Rocky, member secretary of the Shailkupa municipality unit JCD in Jhenaidah.
Mohammad Zahedur Rahman, Officer-in-Charge of Bheramara Police Station, said a group of people hired a boat to visit the Solaiman Shah Shrine in Bheramara from Katla Ghat in Shailkupa of Jhenaidah district.
When the boat was returning after visiting the shrine, it was hit by a strong current, causing it to collide with a pillar of the bridge.
At one point, three people, including Rocky, fell into the river as the rear portion of the bulkhead boat collided with pillar No. 4 of the Hardinge Bridge.
Two of the victims, Liton and Wahab, were rescued, but Rocky remained missing.
Divers from the local fire service conducted a rescue operation but failed to trace Rocky until 1am on Saturday.
Bheramara Upazila Nirbahi Officer Mohammad Amirul Arafat, who visited the scene, said darkness and the strong river current were making the rescue operation difficult, while several government units were working at the scene.
Assistant Director of Kushtia Fire Service and Civil Defence Wadud Hossain said: “Due to the strong current in the Padma, it has become difficult to conduct the search operation at night.”

item.title: ‘CA’ disclaimer sparks customer row at 'Live Shopping' in Mirpur
item.description:
A clothing and accessory shop named “Live Shopping” near Pallabi Metro Station in Dhaka’s Mirpur was closed on Friday afternoon following an altercation between customers and sellers over promotional offer terms.
The incident took place on the fifth floor of the Modern Convention Hall building adjacent to Pallabi Metro Station, where customers had gathered after seeing promotional offers on products at the showroom.
According to police and customers, the showroom used the abbreviation “CA” in small letters under its offers to indicate that terms and conditions applied. Many customers allegedly failed to notice or understand the abbreviation before visiting the showroom to purchase products at the advertised prices.
When sellers informed the customers about the applicable terms and conditions, some became angry and confronted the shopkeepers, leading to an altercation and commotion at the showroom.
Police later went to the scene after receiving the information and spoke to both sides before bringing the situation under control.
The showroom was subsequently closed over allegations that customers had been misled by the promotional offers and the way the applicable terms and conditions were presented.
Meanwhile, Live Shopping claimed that its showroom was looted during the incident.
The company alleged that several people took various products from the showroom. Multiple posts, photos and videos were shared on its Facebook page, “Live Shopping,” seeking help over the alleged looting.
Dhaka Tribune contacted the number provided on the Live Shopping Facebook page for comment but no one answered.
Pallabi police station Officer-in-Charge Hasan Bashir told Dhaka Tribune that the showroom had been selling products under promotional offers while mentioning that terms and conditions applied.
“The establishment adopted a strategy and wrote ‘CA’ in abbreviated form. This escaped the customers’ notice or they could not understand it. After learning about the offer, customers went to the shop and, after learning about the terms and conditions, expressed their anger at the shopkeepers. A commotion broke out. Later, after receiving the information, we went there, spoke to both sides and brought the situation back to normal,” he said.
The OC said the showroom had been temporarily closed and the customers had left.
He said he was not aware of any looting.
“If any customer has been deceived in the incident, they can take legal action,” he said.

item.title: The Mecca Pact faces its first test in Yemen: Where is collective defence?
item.description:
The news that the Houthis have seized control of the strategically vital Yemeni port city of 'Mocha' and the Bab al-Mandab Strait has added a new dimension to the ongoing conflict in the Middle East. The Houthis ousted Saudi-backed government forces to take control of this key Red Sea city, simultaneously securing command over the Bab al-Mandab Strait. This waterway is crucial for trade and energy supplies connecting Asia, Europe, and the Middle East; it has played a vital role, particularly given the potential for the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. According to various international reports, the Houthi advance-marked by the capture of Mocha and missile and drone attacks on Saudi territory-has placed renewed pressure on the oil market.
In this context, a critical question arises: how effective in reality is the trilateral 'Mecca Joint Defense Pact' signed just a month ago by Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, and Turkey? The core principle of the pact is clear—an armed attack on any member state is considered an attack on all three nations. Yet, amidst Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, the retreat of Saudi-backed forces in Yemen, and the loss of Mocha, there has been no visible action from the other members. What is the stance of Pakistan and Turkey in this conflict? Will they truly come to Saudi Arabia's aid? Bangladesh has viewed this pact positively from the outset, with many in the government expressing interest in it. What, then, are the lessons for Bangladesh? Should the country remain positive about joining the Mecca Pact?
The Fall of Mocha: More Than Just a Yemeni City
To grasp the significance of Mocha's capture, one must look at the map. Situated on the Red Sea coast, the port lies near the Bab al-Mandab Strait. Consequently, controlling it does more than shift the military balance of Yemen's civil war; it impacts international maritime routes. The Houthi advance has now reached a point where they can exert pressure on Red Sea shipping and Saudi Arabia's maritime lanes.
In recent days, the Houthis have launched missile and drone attacks on southern Saudi Arabia. According to Saudi authorities, these attacks injured 73 civilians, caused fires at several energy facilities, and temporarily disrupted production. In retaliation, Saudi-led forces have conducted airstrikes on various Houthi-controlled areas in Yemen. In other words, following the informal ceasefire of 2022, Yemen is once again edging towards a major conflict.
The most significant aspect here is that Houthi attacks were a primary concern for regional security even at the time the Mecca Agreement was signed. On August 7, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, and Turkey signed the pact, which stipulated that an armed attack on any one of the three nations would be considered an attack on the other two. Yet, less than a month after the signing, the agreement is facing a real-world test—and it is here that the gap between the political declaration and the actual military commitment is becoming evident."An attack on one is an attack on all"-but what is the reality?
Many have compared the Mecca Agreement to NATO, with some even calling it a "Muslim NATO." However, implementing a defense framework akin to NATO’s Article 5 requires more than just a political declaration; it demands military planning, a command structure, intelligence cooperation, logistical capabilities, and—most crucially—the political will to wage war if necessary. This very question has now arisen regarding the Mecca Agreement.
Following the agreement, Pakistan’s Defense Minister Khawaja Asif warned the Houthis that the pact could be invoked if the conflict spilled over into Saudi territory. Yet, just a day later, Pakistan’s Foreign Ministry clarified that no military action in response to Houthi attacks had been discussed, nor were there plans for immediate military intervention. This rapid shift in stance is highly significant.
This is because Pakistan had already signed a separate "Strategic Mutual Defence Agreement" with Saudi Arabia in September 2025. In exchange, Pakistan got financial support to run the country. That agreement also stipulated that aggression against one nation would be considered aggression against both. But what happened actually? Just in the name of atomic power country they earned some money.
Pakistan did not directly involve itself militarily in the Yemen issue. Never gave support to Saudi Arabia in this case as well. In fact, when Saudi Arabia sought Pakistani troops for its military campaign in Yemen in 2015, Pakistan’s parliament decided to remain neutral in the conflict. The army fully controls Pakistan. Analyses by the Brookings Institution also highlight Pakistan’s long-standing policy of maintaining security cooperation with Saudi Arabia while avoiding direct involvement in the Yemen war.
The question remains- if Pakistan did not directly intervene in the Yemen war even after the 2025 bilateral defense agreement, has the 2026 trilateral Mecca Agreement fundamentally altered that policy? Current realities suggest that no such change is evident, at least in military terms. So the agreement is essentially a deceptive ruse at this moment.
Instead, Pakistan is currently basically taking money, prioritizing diplomatic channels and seeks to avoid direct military involvement. Islamabad has conveyed Saudi Arabia’s message to Iran, urging Tehran to help rein in Houthi attacks. At the same time, Pakistan maintains that the Mecca Agreement is defensive in nature and taking benefits from Saudi Arabia and Turkey. In essence, the practical meaning of the political slogan "an attack on one is an attack on all" remains ambiguous or unimplemented.
Pakistan's past conduct reveals a familiar pattern- it is ready to reap the political, economic, and strategic benefits of its closeness to Saudi Arabia, yet consistently holds back when it comes to paying the actual military price of that relationship.
The Biggest Lesson for Bangladesh: Why Shoulder the Burden of a Distant War?
This is precisely where the most critical aspect of the matter lies for Bangladesh. Bangladesh's security realities differ significantly from those of Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, or Turkey. Bangladesh's primary security and strategic concerns are centered on South Asia. Issues such as borders, the Bay of Bengal, Myanmar, regional trade, maritime security, and economic stability constitute direct realities for the country.
On the other hand, Bangladesh's economy is deeply integrated with international trade, energy imports, remittances, and global supply chains. Consequently, the impact of a Middle East conflict would reach Bangladesh primarily through fluctuations in energy prices, transportation and import costs, remittance flows, and the expatriate labor market. However, the solution to managing these impacts does not lie in becoming militarily entangled in another nation's war.
Rather, the most crucial lesson for Bangladesh is that overcommitting to military alliances that lack a direct link to its own security interests is fraught with risk.
Concepts based on religious identity or the notion of a "collective defense of the Muslim world" may hold political appeal, but they do not align with the core objectives of Bangladesh's foreign policy. Instead, the principle of "Friendship to all, malice towards none" remains the optimal foreign policy stance. At this juncture, our decisions should prioritize national interests, strategic autonomy, and economic development while avoiding conflict. The Mecca Agreement serves as a significant cautionary tale in this regard.
Joining an alliance is easy, but withdrawing when the time comes to honor alliance commitments is difficult. If the conflict involving Saudi Arabia and Yemen escalates, or if Turkey or Pakistan prioritize their own security needs, there is no guarantee regarding the extent of military cooperation that would be provided.
Even the three signatories to the Mecca Agreement are currently emphasizing de-escalation and restraint. While the meeting on August 31 discussed institutionalizing cooperation under the agreement, it simultaneously underscored the importance of a peaceful resolution to the crisis and the reduction of tensions. Ultimately, pragmatic diplomacy prioritizes restraint over warfare—a vital message for Bangladesh.
Bangladesh's Course of Action: Balance, Not Alliances
Bangladesh should view the Middle East conflict as a distant war while closely monitoring its economic repercussions. The security of the Bab al-Mandab Strait and the Red Sea is particularly crucial for Bangladesh, as a vast portion of global trade passes through this region. Consequently, the capture of Mocha and the Houthi advance toward Bab al-Mandab are not merely issues for Saudi Arabia or Yemen; they could impact global supply chains.
Oil prices have already risen, and pressure has mounted on several vital Middle Eastern maritime routes. Should import costs for Bangladesh increase as a result, inflationary pressures could intensify. Beyond fuel imports, transportation costs for the export sector-including the ready-made garment industry-could also be affected.
Therefore, Dhaka’s policy should center on three pillars: strategic balance, economic security, and diplomatic engagement. There is no reason to object to Bangladesh maintaining close ties with Saudi Arabia, enhancing cooperation with Turkey, and cautiously improving relations with Pakistan-mindful of the history of 1971. However, peaceful diplomatic ties and military commitments are not the same thing.
The current reality surrounding the Macca Agreement demonstrates that the ultimate test for a military alliance lies not in the day the pact is signed, but in the moment the first shot is fired.
When Saudi Arabia faced Houthi attacks, Pakistan’s initial response was a diplomatic warning rather than a military operation. Furthermore, following the capture of Mocha, reports emerged that Saudi Arabia was seeking assistance from the United States as it felt the need for greater military support. Where, then, does the "collective defense" aspect of the Macca Agreement stand?
The answer likely lies in the fact that the agreement remains primarily a political signal intended for deterrence, rather than a full-fledged military alliance. Bangladesh must clearly grasp this distinction. Bangladesh does not need to become a party to others' wars; instead, it requires a foreign policy that maintains ties with friends without automatically becoming a participant in any side's conflict.
Ultimately, the most significant lesson of the Mecca Agreement may be this- no matter how grandly a security alliance is proclaimed, its true strength depends on the price its members are willing to pay during a crisis.
For Bangladesh, the path forward should be clear: mitigating the economic fallout of Middle East conflicts, strengthening its diplomatic stance on Red Sea maritime security, and preserving its strategic autonomy while maintaining relations with all parties. For Bangladesh, safeguarding its own peace, security, and economic stability is a far more pragmatic national interest than getting entangled in the wars of others.

item.title: President calls for refit education system based on culture, national needs
item.description:
President Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir on Friday called for a comprehensive overhaul of the country’s education system, aligning it with Bangladesh’s culture, heritage, employment opportunities and national needs.
“We have to restore our education system afresh by combining our literature, heritage, culture, employment opportunities and all other related necessities,” he said when a delegation of Association of Private Universities of Bangladesh (APUB) met him at Bangabhaban.
“The fragile education system left behind by the previous regime must be revamped afresh. It is necessary to introduce an integrated education system by bringing together various types of education systems,” the President said.
He said indiscriminate approval of low-quality educational institutions during the previous regime had contributed to the creation of an unskilled workforce in the country.
Emphasizing the importance of vocational and technical education, the President said such education could help produce skilled manpower, create employment opportunities abroad and increase the country’s foreign exchange earnings.
During the meeting, the APUB delegation apprised the President of the overall development of higher education, the current state of private universities, efforts to develop skilled human resources and the contribution of private universities to the country’s economic progress.
The delegation sought the President’s cooperation in introducing a performance- and results-based evaluation system and approving new universities based on subject-wise demand, national needs, investment capacity and quality standards.
They called for the introduction of updated curricula, internships, apprenticeships, foreign-language education, artificial intelligence (AI) and professional skills training to ensure that graduates are equipped for employment.
The delegation further urged the President to take steps to transform the University Grants Commission (UGC) into a supportive and development-oriented regulatory body and to formulate an integrated national education system.
Praising the contribution of private universities to the country’s development, the President noted that several private universities of Bangladesh have secured positions in global rankings.
As Chancellor of the universities, the President assured the delegation of all-out cooperation for the development of private universities.

item.title: Journalist found dead at Samakal Barisal bureau office
item.description:
Police recovered the hanging body of senior journalist and former Daily Samakal Barisal bureau chief Pulak Chatterjee, 57, from the newspaper’s Barisal bureau office on Friday evening.
The body was recovered from the office on Parara Road in the city.
According to local sources, Pulak Chatterjee had been dismissed from Samakal about three years ago. He was a former general secretary of the Barisal Press Club and had previously worked for Daily Jugantor for many years. He is survived by his wife and a daughter.
Suman Chowdhury, chief staff reporter at Samakal’s Barisal office, said Pulak had a key to the office and often visited it during the day or at night.
“His wife called me in the afternoon and said he was not answering his phone. When I came to the office in the evening, I found the door locked from inside. Looking through a gap, I saw him hanging with a noose around his neck. I immediately informed the police,” he said.
Police later broke open the door and recovered the body.
Pulak had most recently served as Samakal’s Barisal bureau chief. He had reportedly been mentally distressed since losing his job at the newspaper about three years ago.
Al Mamun-ul Islam, officer-in-charge of Barisal Kotwali Model Police Station, said police initially suspected suicide.
“The exact cause of death will be known after the autopsy report,” he said.

item.title: Three held with gold jewellery worth Tk 1.37 crore at Dhaka airport
item.description:
Airport Armed Police Battalion (APBn) detained three people with 861.8 grams of gold jewellery, equivalent to around 74 bhoris, at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport.
The detainees were identified as Md Nasir Molla, 40, Sohag Sheikh, 24, and Md Hasan Mia, 23.
According to APBn, the three were seen moving suspiciously on the footpath on the northern side of the airport roundabout late Thursday night.
Sensing the presence of police, they allegedly tried to flee discreetly, but APBn personnel detained them.
A body search led to the recovery of 861.8 grams of gold jewellery in their possession. The jewellery was made of 21- and 22-carat gold and had an estimated market value of Tk 1,36,86,160.
During preliminary interrogation, the detainees reportedly said the jewellery had been brought into Bangladesh from different countries through unidentified passengers for the purpose of smuggling.
APBn said the three had allegedly been involved in gold smuggling at the airport for a long time.
A regular case was filed against them with the Airport Police Station on Thursday.
The case alleges that the three, in collusion with one another and with the assistance of unidentified passengers, brought the gold into the country illegally for smuggling while evading government revenue and kept it in their possession.
Mohammad Rezaul Kabir, superintendent of police of Airport (13) APBn, said the force remains committed to maintaining security at the airport and preventing crime.
“We remain active and vigilant in preventing smuggling and controlling other crimes. Airport APBn is determined to prevent gold and drug smuggling, and our operations to stop any form of smuggling through the airport will continue,” he said.

item.title: Eggs, vegetables turn costlier as prices rise by Tk10-40
item.description:
Prices of eggs and several vegetables have increased in Dhaka markets over the past week, while fish and meat prices have remained largely stable.
A dozen eggs, which sold for Tk145-150 last week, are now priced at Tk155-160, marking a Tk10 increase. Retailers are selling individual eggs for around Tk13-14.
Among vegetables, green chilli and yardlong bean prices have risen by Tk40 per kg each to Tk160 and Tk120, respectively. Round eggplant has increased by Tk20 to Tk140 per kg, while cucumber has risen by Tk20-30 to Tk80.
However, tomato and papaya prices have fallen. Tomatoes now sell for Tk100 per kg, down from Tk120-140, while papaya has dropped from Tk40 to Tk30.
Prices of ridge gourd, bitter gourd, sponge gourd, snake gourd and pointed gourd have remained largely unchanged at around Tk80 per kg.
The situation was observed during visits to several markets in the capital on Friday.
Meanwhile, fish prices showed no major changes. Sellers said prices of some varieties fluctuate by Tk20-30 per kg from one day to another.
Pangash is selling for Tk230 per kg, telapia Tk260, shrimp Tk800-900, pabda Tk350-450, large rui Tk450-500 and tengra Tk700.
Vetki is priced at Tk400-550 per kg, mrigel Tk250-300, baim Tk600-800, local koi Tk700-800, farmed koi Tk300 and poa Tk260. Farmed shing is selling for Tk300-450 per kg depending on size, while medium-sized rui costs Tk270-350.
When asked about fish prices, Sheikh Rafiqul said, “I bought fish for the month. Prices seem Tk20-30 higher per kilogram. The fish market is never stable, with prices fluctuating almost every day.”
The price hike has put the greatest strain on low-income and limited-income households. Abul Hossain, a day labourer, said, “We used to buy pangas and telapia, but even those have become expensive. Prices are rising day by day, with no sign of coming down.”
Meanwhile, beef is being sold at Tk800 per kilogram, almost unchanged from the previous week. Broiler chicken is also being sold at Tk180-190 per kilogram, the same as last week. However, prices of Sonali, hybrid and layer chickens have fallen by around Tk10 per kilogram.
Rocky Ahmed, a chicken seller at Rayerbazar, said, “Chicken prices were slightly lower this week than last week. Still, we are selling them at Tk180-190 per kilogram.”
Egg trader Masum said, “Egg prices have not fallen; rather, they have increased. A dozen eggs are now selling for Tk155-160.”
Zahidur Rahman, a private-sector employee who came to Raysahib Bazar to shop on his weekly day off, said, “I found vegetable prices considerably higher than last week. Many vegetables that were available at lower prices last week are now more expensive. This is naturally increasing our household expenses.”
Rafiqullah Khan, a vegetable seller at Narinda Bazar, attributed the price rise to reduced supply following several days of rain.
“Several days of rain have reduced the supply of vegetables from farms and markets. Lower supply has pushed up wholesale prices, which has affected retail prices as well,” he said.
“Eggplant is currently selling at Tk140 per kilogram, the highest price in today’s market, while papaya is available at Tk30 per kilogram. If the weather improves, supply will increase and vegetable prices may come down,” he added.

item.title: Measles outbreak: Death toll reaches 1,012 as three die in 24 hours
item.description:
Three more children have died from measles-like symptoms in the 24 hours leading up to 8:00am on Friday, raising the overall death toll from the ongoing outbreak to 1,012.
The Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) has classified all three of the latest casualties as suspected.
With the latest figures, the total number of suspected measles deaths has reached 912, while the number of confirmed deaths remained unchanged at 100, as no new confirmed measles deaths were reported in the last 24 hours.
Among the latest suspected fatalities, Chittagong division recorded the highest count with two deaths.
A total of 1,077 suspected measles cases were recorded in the 24 hours till Friday morning, taking the overall suspected case tally to 169,822.
During the same period, 34 new confirmed measles cases were reported, bringing the total number of confirmed infections to 19,967.

item.title: Flour, aromatic rice prices spike as edible oil crisis persists in Dhaka
item.description:
Prices of flour, refined flour (maida) and aromatic rice have risen sharply in Dhaka kitchen markets, adding to pressure on bakeries, biryani businesses and middle-income households amid a continued shortage of soybean oil.
A visit to markets in Shantinagar, Rampura, Badda and Shahjadpur on Friday found loose flour selling at Tk50 per kg, up from Tk45 last week, while the maida price climbed to Tk80-85 per kg from Tk70-75.
Aromatic rice prices jumped by Tk20 per kg even after the Ministry of Commerce halved the export quota for the variety. Quality loose aromatic rice is now selling at Tk200 per kg, up from Tk180 a week earlier, while packaged aromatic rice ranges between Tk220 and Tk240 per kg. Buyers said the same rice cost only Tk150-160 per kg a month ago.
More than a week after soybean oil prices were raised, supply has yet to return to normal. Most shops are out of bottled one-litre soybean oil, forcing many buyers to purchase costlier rice bran or sunflower oil instead.
Retailers said repeated requests to oil companies and dealers for supply have gone unanswered, adding that their per-litre commission has been cut.
They also alleged several companies are withholding soybean oil unless retailers place orders for other products alongside it.
Bakery and biryani businesses warned they will be forced to raise prices further if the trend continues.
Anwar, manager of Maa Biriyani in Badda, said they used to sell chicken polao at Tk120 per packet but now charge Tk150, adding that even the new price may soon become difficult to sustain amid the continued rise in costs.
Adib Rahman, owner of Adib Live Bakery in Rampura, said bakery associations have asked members to raise prices of all maida-based products by 20%, noting that not raising prices erodes profit while raising them drives away customers.
Buyers blamed both global volatility and a lack of government market monitoring for the price spikes, saying reduced oil supply and indiscriminate flour price hikes cannot be justified.
"There is no point in market monitoring for show. Why are not big corporate companies supplying oil to the market? They must be held accountable, otherwise consumer interest will remain ignored while companies protect only their own," said Afsana, a consumer at Rampura market.
Another buyer, Imdad, said grocery bills are rising every month due to price hikes across the board, compounding pressure from higher electricity costs on middle-income families like his.
According to the Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics (BBS), overall inflation stood at 8.26% in August, with food inflation at 7.02%. Though overall inflation eased compared to July, buyers say the relief is not visible in the market.

item.title: Health minister vows strict action over hospital irregularities
item.description:
Health Minister Sardar Md Sakhawat Husain on Friday said he would take a strict stance against irregularities in hospitals during an inspection of Mugda Medical College Hospital in Dhaka.
He said: “Either I will remain, or irregularities in hospitals will.”
During the inspection, the minister found evidence supporting complaints that patients were being sent outside for medical tests despite the hospital having facilities to conduct blood and other tests under government management.
He visited different wards, spoke to patients and their relatives, and examined medical documents and test reports.
Sardar Md Sakhawat Husain said: “The complaint I heard and came here to investigate is 100% true. Despite government hospitals having testing facilities to detect dengue, I found evidence that people from outside diagnostic centers were coming and collecting blood samples from patients.”
He said: “There are facilities here. People come from outside and take blood from here. Are they blind? There are doctors here. Will they not see?”
The minister said: “The government has arrangements to provide necessary tests to patients free of charge. Even after that, if people from outside come and collect samples from patients, we will investigate who is involved.”
During the visit, patients and their relatives also told the minister about various problems at the hospital. They particularly complained that the lifts are not operated regularly, forcing patients and relatives to move between different floors for tests.
The health minister also spoke about the dengue situation. He said hospitals are prepared to handle the pressure of dengue patients and that treatment capacity would be increased if the number of patients rises.
He said nationwide cleanliness and preventive campaigns would also be strengthened to prevent dengue.
The minister said field inspections to identify irregularities in the health sector would continue.

item.title: Missing businessman found buried beneath friend’s house in Lalbagh
item.description:
The body of a 47-year-old man, who went missing three days ago, was recovered from beneath a house in Lalbagh, Dhaka, on Friday.
Police also detained Roni’s friend Masum, 46, in connection with the incident.
Police said Masum killed Roni after Roni demanded repayment of Tk3 lakh owed to him. Masum was initially detained and questioned as a suspect after Roni went missing and later admitted to killing and burying him, police said.
Following information provided by Masum, police recovered Roni’s partially decomposed body from an open space on the ground floor of a 5-storey building at Holding No 9 on BC Das Street under Ward 26.
His hands and legs were tied, while his face was wrapped in polythene, police said.
Inspector (Investigation) Md Saiduzzaman of Lalbagh Police Station said Roni had been missing for three days and his brother, Sheikh Abdul Karim, had filed a general diary (GD) with the police station.
He said police began investigating the disappearance and brought Masum to the police station for questioning based on the call records of Roni’s mobile phone.
Masum had also gone to the police station when the GD was filed, the police official said.
During questioning, Masum admitted that Roni was owed Tk3 lakh by him and had been pressuring him to repay the money.
Masum then took Roni to his house on the pretext of paying the money, police said. He allegedly struck Roni on the head, knocking him down, before tying his hands and legs, wrapping his face in polythene and burying him under sand and soil in an empty space between two buildings beneath the house.
Following Masum’s instructions, police went to the location and recovered Roni’s partially decomposed body by digging through the sand and soil.
After completing legal procedures, police sent the body to the morgue of Dhaka Medical College Hospital on Friday morning for an autopsy.
Roni lived in Khilgaon, police said.
The police official said Roni’s wife, Nusrat Jahan Sima, filed a case with the police station as the complainant.

item.title: Rare clouded leopard photographed in Cox’s Bazar forest
item.description:
A rare clouded leopard has been photographed in Bangladesh’s Inani National Park in Cox’s Bazar, providing new evidence of the species’ persistence in one of the country’s fragmented forest landscapes.
The photograph was captured during a wildlife survey conducted between November 2022 and November 2023, according to a study titled “Mammalian persistence and conservation priorities in a fragmented tropical refuge of Bangladesh,” published in the Journal for Nature Conservation on March 18, 2026.
Researchers surveyed 32 sites across the 7,085-hectare national park using 15 camera traps and recorded 23 species of wild mammals.
Photo: Courtesy
The clouded leopard (Neofelis nebulosa) was detected at three locations, with 13 photographs recorded across 9 detection events, the study said.
Researchers estimated the species’ occupancy at 0.24, indicating that it was present in roughly one-quarter of the surveyed area.
The survey also recorded several other species important for conservation, including Asian elephants, western hoolock gibbons, capped langurs, leopard cats, jungle cats and hog badgers.
Bipul Krishna Das, director of the Bangladesh Wildlife Center of the Forest Department and lead author of the study, said the survey used 15 camera traps at 32 sites in Inani National Park.
The researchers found that habitat condition was closely linked to mammal diversity in the park. Areas with more natural forest supported greater wildlife diversity, while plantations and heavily altered areas supported less.
The study said the clouded leopard is regarded as Critically Endangered in Bangladesh, while the International Union for Conservation of Nature classifies the species as Vulnerable globally.
It found that Inani serves as a refuge and corridor for threatened mammals in southeastern Bangladesh, while cautioning that the forest remains under pressure from human activities.
Deforestation, forest encroachment and livestock grazing can degrade and fragment habitats, reducing the area suitable for wildlife, the researchers said.
They recommended restoring degraded areas with native vegetation, strengthening protection along vulnerable forest boundaries and involving local communities in conservation efforts.
The researchers also stressed the importance of closely monitoring wildlife in the park to better understand how threatened species use the fragmented forest landscape.
The study was conducted by researchers from Bangladesh and Germany and was published in Volume 92 of the Journal for Nature Conservation.

item.title: Two bikers killed in separate road accidents in Barisal
item.description:
Two motorcycle riders were killed and another was critically injured in separate road accidents in Gournadi upazila of Barisal on Friday.
Arafat Rahman Babu, 32, was killed and his pillion rider Asadul Islam, 31, was critically injured when a bus crashed into their bike in front of Sharmin Clinic in South Bijoypur around 10:30am.
Babu, a father of two, was a resident of Ashokathi village and the foster son of retired teacher Md Hanif Akon, who currently lives in Mahilara. Asadul is also from Ashokathi village
Following the accident, locals rescued them and took them to a nearby upazila health complex, where doctors declared Babu dead.
Asadul was later shifted to Sher-e-Bangla Medical College Hospital in critical condition.
In another accident, Mehedi Hasan Turag, 32, was killed in the Kataksthal area around 2:30am. Turag was the son of deceased Abdul Gani Howlader of Rajkar area under Rahmatpur union of Babuganj upazila.
According to Turag’s friend Tarikul Islam, four friends were travelling from Dhaka to their village home in Babuganj on two motorcycles.

item.title: Yemen’s Houthis take over strait vital to global shipping
item.description:
Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis seized a strategic Red Sea island on Friday after capturing territory along the coast, sealing their takeover of a vital shipping corridor linking Europe and Asia.
The development is likely to deepen the Middle East war’s impact on international commerce, months after the strategic Strait of Hormuz was blockaded by Iran, which hailed its Yemeni allies’ advance on Friday.
After a week-long offensive that has left hundreds dead, the Houthis appeared to be in control of territory along the Yemeni side of the Bab al-Mandab Strait, the southern gateway to the Red Sea and, in turn, the Suez Canal.
A local official with Yemen’s Saudi-backed government said on Friday that the Houthis had “completed their takeover of the Bab al-Mandab area and Mayyun Island,” while a witness said gunmen were “deploying along the Bab al-Mandab shore and are driving around in military vehicles.”
The capture of Mayyun Island, in the middle of the narrow waterway, heightens the fighters’ ability to attack Saudi tankers, which they have been targeting since July.
Saudi Arabia, the world’s biggest oil exporter, has relied on the Red Sea ever since Iran’s Hormuz blockade choked off its shipments via the Gulf.
Mohammad Mokhber, an adviser to Iranian supreme leader Mojtaba Khamenei, congratulated the Houthis on their “resounding victory” on Friday.
“Now the Iranians don’t only control Hormuz and the Strait of Hormuz, but they control the other most strategic chokepoint in the Middle East,” Farea Al-Muslimi, research fellow at the Chatham House think-tank, told AFP.
Oil prices have soared past $100 a barrel this week, while average US diesel prices topped $6 for the first time on Friday -- a potential headache for President Donald Trump ahead of midterm elections.
A member of the Houthis’ politburo had sought to allay fears for global shipping in an interview released on Friday, insisting “there is no cause for international concern.”
“Freedom of navigation and international trade in the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandab are safe and orderly,” Hazem al-Assad told the Al-Araby al-Jadeed news outlet.
The Houthi offensive has cost more than 500 lives and has displaced about 46,000 people, the UN migration agency said on Friday.
It is part of renewed hostilities in divided Yemen’s brutal civil war that began with the group’s takeover of the capital Sanaa in 2014.
The Houthis carried out their heaviest missile and drone attack in years this week against Saudi Arabia -- Yemen’s northern neighbor -- setting oil sites ablaze and wounding 73.
Satellite images from Copernicus Sentinel Data taken on Thursday showed black smoke billowing near Medina, along the general route of the East-West pipeline that carries Saudi oil to its Red Sea coast.
Before the Red Sea offensive, the Houthis already controlled a large part of Yemen’s north.
They have recently attacked government-held areas in Hodeida and Taiz provinces and swept down the coast, seizing the port city of Mocha and Zuqar island, north of the Bab al-Mandab, on Thursday.
Mohamed, 46, who fled Mocha in the middle of the night, told AFP there was an “apocalyptic” atmosphere in the historic city.
While Saudi Arabia has hit back with airstrikes and ordered troop reinforcements from Aden, where the internationally recognized government is based, it has failed to stop the Houthis’ lightning advance.
Houthi media said two Saudi strikes hit Mocha’s airport on Friday, while a local official there said the city’s seaport was also hit by six missiles of unknown origin.
“I think the Saudis have tried everything they can to avoid this war, but I don’t think they have any more choice,” said Al-Muslimi.
The local Yemeni official said the number of fighters on Mayyun island, just 13 square kilometers (five square miles) was “not large,” adding that they would probably deploy on hills overlooking the Bab al-Mandab.
The strait has four strategic islands: Zuqar and Mayyun, both in Houthi control, and the two Hanish islands. Government military sources told AFP that the Houthis have besieged government troops on the Hanish islands.
The UN Security Council met Thursday to discuss the conflict with Yemen envoy Hans Grundberg, who called for “the active investment of every member of this body to contain” what could become a more dangerous conflict.
The ongoing exchanges risk reviving a war that killed hundreds of thousands of Yemenis and sparked one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises.
The Houthis, after seizing Sanaa and forcing out the government, fought a Saudi-led coalition from 2015 until a United Nations-brokered ceasefire in 2022.
